newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto 'cynical' about talks with India.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto 'cynical' about talks with India.

text.p: Pakistani opposition leader Benazir Bhutto said on Friday she was "cynical" about the outcome of current Indo-Pakistan peace talks in Islamabad.

The former prime minister told Reuters Television she was disappointed that India did not make even a symbolic gesture towards the people of the disputed layan region of Kashmir at Friday's resumption of a dialogue launched last March.

"I had hoped that political prisoners who had been in jail for a very long time, particularly those who need medical attention, would have been freed," she said about militants arrested for opposing Indian rule over two-thirds of Kashmir.
"Of course everybody is happy about the talks," Bhutto said in the interview after top Indian and Pakistani foreign ministry officials met for two hours at the start of four-day talks.

"But I am cynical about them leading anywhere because India has failed to make even a symbolic gesture regarding the core issue of Jammu and Kashmir even in purely human terms such as the release of political prisoners," she said.
Pakistan controls a third of the region, over which the two countries have fought two of their three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Bhutto's government, which was sacked by President Farooq Leghari last November on disputed charges of misrule, had made it a condition for resuming peace that India reduce what Islamabad calls repression in Kashmir.
"I think, to be cosntructive, the talks should have two agendas -- one with regard to the Kashmir dispute and one with regard to Pakistan-India problems."

About Kashmir, she said there should be charter for the release of all political prisoners, withdrawal of "repressive rules", withdrawal of armed forces there and then discussion on solving the problem on the basis of U.N. resolutions.

On Indo-Pakistan problem, Bhutto said the two countries should agree on non-deployment of missiles against each other and to begin talks on a "zero-missile regime" because both could develop missiles.

"I think time has shown that India exploded a nuclear bomb and then Pakistan acquired the knowledge (to make it)," she said referring to India's explosion of what it called a peaceful nuclear explosion in 1974.
"Time has shown that India acquired missile technology and Pakistan did the same. So it's about time that we stop upping the ante and agree to bilateral non-proliferation regime."

Earlier, an official Pakistani spokesman for the talks said the two sides were very hopeful that they would be able to devise a mechanism for future for future meetings between the arch-rival neighbours.
